title: Weekly Brief

scope.disclosure: This brief uses public industry sources and does not assess Proterra-owned animals, customers, sales, or commercial performance.

executiveSummary: New U.S. data show higher second-quarter milk output and replacement-cow prices alongside firm cattle and beef values. Boxed beef and live cattle strengthened, retail and farm beef values increased from the first quarter, and processing-beef volume rose even as lean-trim prices eased.
editorNote: The reviewed evidence queue supported five U.S. developments: one dairy and four meat. The editorial override accepts the absence of bovine-genetics and international candidates; no Latin America or Puerto Rico candidate was available. The dashboard is omitted because the evidence cannot support a bovine-genetics pulse without filler.

overview.headline: U.S. milk output and cattle values moved higher across the latest releases.

points.label: Dairy
points.text: Second-quarter milk production, cow numbers, milk per cow, and replacement-cow prices all exceeded year-earlier levels.

points.label: Beef
points.text: Choice and Select boxed-beef averages rose from the prior week, with the Choice premium reaching $23.06 per hundredweight.

points.label: Cattle
points.text: Five-area live-steer and live-heifer prices increased from the prior week as reported negotiated volume expanded.

items.headline: U.S. dairy production and cow numbers exceed year-earlier levels
items.summary: USDA's updated dairy tables put second-quarter 2026 milk production at 60.194 billion pounds, compared with 58.783 billion pounds a year earlier. The milk-cow herd, milk per cow, feed value, and replacement-cow price also exceeded their second-quarter 2025 levels.
keyPoints: The April-June milk-cow herd averaged 9.666 million head, up from 9.474 million in the same 2025 quarter.
Milk per cow was 6,227 pounds, compared with 6,205 pounds a year earlier.
The replacement-cow price reached $3,130 per head, up from $2,860 per head.
items.whyItMatters: More cows and slightly higher output per cow combined to lift national milk production, while higher replacement values raised the cost benchmark for herd expansion.
items.businessRelevance: If these conditions persist, dairy producers may weigh higher replacement values against the productivity and longevity expected from breeding decisions. The national figures are market context, not evidence of uniform farm economics.
items.uncertainty: Quarterly national totals do not show regional margins or establish whether the year-over-year expansion will continue through the second half.
items.watchNext: Watch the next USDA dairy tables for herd growth, milk per cow, and replacement prices.

citations.title: Dairy Monthly Tables and Dairy Quarterly Data
citations.sourceNote: The USDA ERS tables provide the second-quarter 2025 and 2026 milk-production, herd, yield, feed-value, and replacement-price observations used here.

items.headline: Choice boxed beef rises faster than Select in the latest week
items.summary: The negotiated Choice 600-900 pound boxed-beef cutout averaged $373.24 per hundredweight for the week of August 14, up $6.73 from the prior week. Select averaged $350.18, up $1.95, leaving a $23.06 Choice-Select spread.
keyPoints: Choice negotiated volume totaled 292.70 loads, while Select volume totaled 85.74 loads.
The Choice weekly average increased by $6.73 per hundredweight versus a $1.95 increase for Select.
The resulting Choice-Select spread was $23.06 per hundredweight.
items.whyItMatters: The wider quality spread provides a current market measure of the premium attached to Choice product in negotiated wholesale trade.
items.businessRelevance: If the premium persists, it may reinforce producer and processor attention to carcass-quality outcomes. One weekly report should not be treated as a lasting change in beef demand or cattle returns.
items.uncertainty: The release covers negotiated weekly sales and does not establish retail demand, processor margins, or the durability of the quality spread.
items.watchNext: Watch the next weekly cutout for whether Choice holds its gain and whether the spread remains above $23 per hundredweight.

citations.title: National Weekly Boxed Beef Cutout & Boxed Beef Cuts - Negotiated Sales (LM_XB459)
citations.sourceNote: This release supplies the Choice and Select weekly cutout averages, prior-week changes, negotiated volumes, and Choice-Select spread.

items.headline: Retail beef value and the farm share rise in the second quarter
items.summary: USDA's meat price-spread data show second-quarter Choice beef retail value at 1,042.3 cents per pound of retail equivalent, up from 1,004.2 cents in the first quarter. Net farm value rose to 568.4 cents, and the farmer's share increased to 54.5 percent from 53.7 percent.
keyPoints: Choice beef wholesale value rose to 581.1 cents per pound of retail equivalent from 566.6 cents in the first quarter.
The wholesale-to-retail spread increased to 461.2 cents per pound from 437.6 cents.
The five-market steer price increased to $254.72 per hundredweight from $238.96.
items.whyItMatters: The series shows that farm, wholesale, retail, and spread values all moved higher between the first and second quarters rather than rising at a single stage.
items.businessRelevance: The higher farm share and steer price may support producer confidence, but breeding investment still depends on local costs and expected returns. These aggregate values are context rather than a direct demand forecast.
items.uncertainty: Quarterly price spreads summarize national market stages and do not identify the cause of the changes or the margins earned by individual businesses.
items.watchNext: Watch third-quarter retail, wholesale, net farm, and farmer-share observations for confirmation or reversal.

citations.title: Meat Price Spreads
citations.sourceNote: The USDA ERS dataset provides comparable first- and second-quarter Choice beef values, price spreads, farmer share, and five-market steer prices.

items.headline: Five-area live cattle prices and negotiated volume increase
items.summary: USDA's five-area report listed 83,721 head for the latest completed week, compared with 26,255 a week earlier and 47,342 in the comparable year-earlier period. Live steer and heifer weighted averages both exceeded the preceding week's levels.
keyPoints: Live steers averaged $235.21 per hundredweight across 33,571 head, versus $233.06 across 8,785 head a week earlier.
Live heifers averaged $235.05 per hundredweight across 7,620 head, versus $232.57 across 3,721 head.
Dressed steers averaged $371.11 and dressed heifers $370.18 per hundredweight.
items.whyItMatters: The report pairs higher weekly cattle prices with a larger negotiated sample, providing a stronger current benchmark for the five-area fed-cattle market.
items.businessRelevance: If fed-cattle values remain firm, producers may have more room to evaluate breeding and replacement investments. The market report does not establish net profitability after feed and other costs.
items.uncertainty: Weekly negotiated volume can vary sharply with trading timing, so the increase should not be projected forward from one release.
items.watchNext: Watch the next five-area report for price persistence, negotiated head count, and live-versus-dressed trade mix.

citations.title: 5 Area Weekly Weighted Average Direct Slaughter Cattle (LM_CT150)
citations.sourceNote: This release provides latest-week, prior-week, and year-earlier head counts plus live and dressed steer and heifer weighted averages.

items.headline: Processing-beef trade volume rises as lean-trim values ease
items.summary: National processing-beef volume reached 6,686,309 pounds in the August 14 release, up from 6,179,616 pounds in the previous release. Average values eased for both fresh 90 percent lean processing beef and fresh 50 percent lean trim.
keyPoints: Fresh 90 percent lean processing beef averaged $455.14 per hundredweight across 42 trades and 1,279,012 pounds.
The prior-release average for fresh 90 percent lean product was $455.87 per hundredweight.
Fresh 50 percent lean trim averaged $144.89 per hundredweight across 68 trades and 1,570,520 pounds, down from $150.46.
items.whyItMatters: Higher reported volume alongside lower lean-product averages distinguishes active trade from price strength in the processing-beef market.
items.businessRelevance: Lean-beef and trim values can help frame downstream demand for beef production. The mixed volume-and-price signal should be used as context, not as a direct forecast for cattle or genetics demand.
items.uncertainty: The comparison covers two releases and does not establish a sustained trend or explain whether supply, demand, or product mix drove the price changes.
items.watchNext: Watch the next release for whether volume remains elevated and whether 50 and 90 percent lean values stabilize.
